scenario: AITA for adopting a puppy when we were notified the foster wanted to adopt the puppy, we were notified after a week of adotion process | My fiancee, her son (9), and I just moved into a new house and finally have no restrictions on owning a dog. We have applied for several puppies through a local rescue/adoption agency. After sending 8 or 10 applications for various puppies and being put on waitlists we finally got the call that we were set for an interview. We had initially been second in line but something from the first interview didn't work out so we moved up to first in line the day after our application. We did an interview the next day and everything went well and the adoption coordinator said they would notify the foster home. The puppy had a final medical check for a small hip injury on the following Tuesday. On Monday we got an email from the foster family to start the process of setting up a meet and greet. Tuesday afternoon we got a call from the agency that the medical went well and the puppy is healthy. But they also told us that the foster was apparently interested in adopting the dog. Typically the foster homes get first choice for adopting dogs they foster and the puppy should apparently never have been listed. The agency says they have bonded between the family and puppy. Because it was an error on the part of the agency and the puppy should never have been listed as available for adoptions, they have left the choice with us to either follow through and adopt the puppy or allow the foster family to keep the puppy. We have been excited about this puppy since last Wednesday when we were first selected for an interview. Have already bought a collar and several toys for her and shown her to friends and family and told them we were in the process of adopting this beautiful puppy. Our nine year old son also loves the dog and is crushed by the news we may not get her now. Am I the asshole if we adopted the puppy and didn't let the foster family keep her?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm "the asshole" in this situation. Let me start by understanding what happened. We moved into a new house and finally have no restrictions on owning a dog. That's great! We applied for several puppies through a local rescue/adoption agency. We sent out 8 or 10 applications and got put on waitlists. Finally, we got a call that we were set for an interview. Initially, we were second in line, but something from the first interview didn't work out, so we moved up to first in line the day after our application. We did the interview the next day, and everything went well. The adoption coordinator said they would notify the foster home. The puppy had a final medical check for a small hip injury on the following Tuesday. On Monday, we got an email from the foster family to start the process of setting up a meet-and-greet. Tuesday afternoon, we got a call from the agency that the medical went well, and the puppy is healthy. But they also told us that the foster was apparently interested in adopting the dog. Typically, foster homes get first choice for adopting dogs they foster, and the puppy should apparently never have been listed. The agency said there was a bond between the family and the puppy. Because it was an error on the part of the agency and the puppy should never have been listed as available for adoption, they left the choice with us to either follow through and adopt the puppy or allow the foster family to keep the puppy. We've been excited about this puppy since last Wednesday when we were first selected for an interview. We've already bought a collar and several toys for her and shown her to friends and family, telling them we were in the process of adopting this beautiful puppy. Our nine-year-old son also loves the dog and is crushed by the news that we may not get her now. So, the question is: Am I the asshole if we adopt the puppy and didn't let the foster family keep her? First, I need to understand the dynamics here. Foster homes usually have the first choice to adopt the animals they care for. That makes sense because they've already invested time and emotional energy into the animal. It's a common practice in adoption processes to give foster families priority. In this case, the agency made a mistake by listing the puppy as available for adoption when it shouldn't have been. That's a procedural error on their part. They've now given us the choice to either proceed with the adoption or allow the foster family to keep the puppy. We've already invested emotionally and financially into this puppy. We've told our friends and family about her, and our son is really excited. It's understandable that we're upset and want to proceed with the adoption. On the other hand, the foster family has likely formed a bond with the puppy, and they were supposed to have the first choice. The agency's mistake complicates things because now we're in a position where we have to make a decision that affects both parties. I think the key here is to consider the intentions and the impact on all parties involved. The foster family was supposed to have the first option, and the agency's error put us in a position where we're now making a decision that wasn't supposed to be ours. If we proceed with the adoption, we're taking the puppy away from the foster family, who had the initial right to adopt. That could be seen as unfair, especially since the agency's mistake led to this situation. On the other hand, if we allow the foster family to keep the puppy, we're respecting the usual process and acknowledging the agency's error. However, we've already made significant emotional and financial investments. It's tough to let go of something we've been looking forward to, especially when it involves our child's happiness. I think the right approach would be to communicate openly with the foster family and the agency. Express our feelings and see if there's a way to resolve this that's fair to everyone. Maybe the agency can help facilitate a discussion or find another puppy that's a good match for us. In the end, it's important to balance our own desires with the established practices and the feelings of the foster family. While it's hard, respecting the process and the foster family's initial right might be the more considerate choice, even if it means we have to start over with another puppy.
